title: US summer 2026 flight disruptions: what you're actually owed
summary: See how US airports and travel days compared this summer, and find out if your flight to, from, or within Europe, the UK, or beyond qualifies for compensation.
body_markdown:
If your flight was **delayed** or **canceled** this summer — especially if your trip touched Europe, the UK, or another region with strong passenger-rights laws — **there's a good chance you're owed compensation for it.**


Between June and August 2026, more than 261.9 million passengers flew within, to, or from the US. Of those, 76.7 million — 29.3% of everyone who flew — faced a delay or cancellation, up from 28.4% the summer before. Nearly 3.8 million passengers had a flight canceled within 30 days of departure.


Here's how the summer played out at the airport level, when things were worst (and best), and how you can tell if you're one of the many US travelers who's actually owed money.


## Which month had the roughest disruptions?


July was the toughest month by far, with 31.2% of passengers affected — noticeably worse than June (27.7%) or August (28.8%).


## What were the best and worst days to fly this summer?


July 19 was the single worst day of the summer, with **41.3% of passengers hit by a delay or cancellation** , closely followed by July 18 at 40.5% — back-to-back bad days for anyone flying that weekend.


The best day, perhaps surprisingly, came late in the season: August 25, when just **11.7% of passengers faced any disruption at all** — the calmest day in the entire dataset.

## Which major airports had it worst — and best?


**Dallas Fort Worth** had the toughest summer of any major US hub, with 36.6% of passengers affected, followed by Nashville (35.4%), Reagan National (34.9%), LaGuardia (34.7%), and Chicago O'Hare (34.3%).


**Minneapolis−St Paul** and **Salt Lake City** fared best among the country's busiest airports, with disruption rates of 23.2% and 22.2% respectively.


## How did the US compare with Europe?


The US's 29.3% disruption rate **was slightly higher than Europe's** 27.5% this summer (around 91.6 million passengers affected across the continent). The UK sat close behind Europe's average, at 28%.


## Am I owed compensation for a disrupted flight to, from, or within Europe, the UK, or beyond?


The US doesn't have a fixed compensation law for ordinary delays — but plenty of US travelers still qualify for compensation under someone else's. If your trip this summer touched **a region with developed air passenger rights** — the UK, the EU, Turkey, Brazil, or Saudi Arabia — and your flight **was delayed** by three hours or more, or **canceled** with less than two weeks' notice, **you could be entitled to compensation under that region's rules** , even though you're flying to, from, or within the US.


That covers more trips than you might think: a US-to-London flight delayed on departure, a connecting flight through Frankfurt, a Saudi-operated route into JFK, or a flight to Rio that got canceled — all fall under rules written to protect passengers, not just residents.


Just like in Europe, the amount depends on how far you were flying and how long the delay was.
